prize_parts.citation: For the development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: Palladium-catalysed C-N coupling is a clean, two-person, chemically original achievement. Aryl amine formation went from a harsh and narrow transformation to a routine, general bond construction through successive ligand generations and a mechanistic understanding of oxidative addition, amine binding and reductive elimination. Its adoption is visible in countless later syntheses, in pharmaceutical discovery and in process chemistry at scale. The mechanism is settled, independent confirmation is overwhelming, and there is no question about what was new chemically. It is also the one shortlisted candidate that sits squarely in molecule-making, which the committee has honoured often but where the core of the discipline is underrepresented in this shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the 2010 prize for palladium cross-coupling in C-C bond formation already honoured the Pd-coupling paradigm, so C-N coupling can be read as a natural but partly redundant extension. Support in the openings is also narrow: only Zou and I ranked it, and Zou placed it seventh. Kosugi's earlier tin-amide work leaves a small precedence question. I am working from memory on precedence details and have not verified them. If most colleagues consider the practical impact insufficient to overcome the 2010 overlap, the committee should move to a candidate with broader support.

responses.point: Zou ranked C-N coupling seventh and considers its originality somewhat reduced by the 2010 Pd cross-coupling prize, although it is thoroughly confirmed and industrially embedded.
responses.response: The 2010 prize covered C-C coupling of organometallic partners with organic halides. Making C-N bonds with amines required different ligand design, because the amine binds the metal and beta-hydride elimination competes with reductive elimination. Buchwald and Hartwig solved that problem. The relationship to 2010 is real, but the C-N problem was not an obvious corollary, and I do not think it is closer to redundancy than the 2001 hydrogenation and oxidation prizes were to each other. I would still count it as a fair objection to weigh, and I thank Zou for agreeing that attribution to the two laureates is clear.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks targeted protein degradation first, as a simple chemical idea with a game-changing consequence that opens the undruggable proteome, and accepts that approved drugs are still few.
responses.response: I share the admiration for the PROTAC concept, but I qualify the claim that it is chemistry-simple and consequential in the same sense. The new element is the design idea of induced proximity, while the molecules themselves are largely modular medicinal chemistry, and no degrader is yet an established drug class. C-N coupling has already delivered its consequences over decades. I also see the allocation problem he flags as serious. Crews, Deshaies, Handa and Ciulli each have a legitimate claim to credit and I do not see a fair trio, so B042 is my second choice rather than my first.

responses.point: Linke ranks base editing first for its clear chemical principle (deamination within an editing window) plus a general capability, and ranks sequencing technology second while asking what is new in the chemistry.
responses.response: I agree with his own test of stating what is new chemically, and I apply it to B050. Deaminase chemistry was known, so the novelty is the fusion to a programmable Cas scaffold and the directed evolution of TadA for adenine editing. That is an impressive invention but sits close to the 2020 CRISPR prize and is only about a decade old. I take the maturity point seriously. I would not oppose B050 if the committee wants a biology-adjacent prize, but I think it is premature relative to a mature, fully tested method, and I am uneasy about naming trainees such as Komor and Gaudelli alongside Liu without committee-level agreement on principle.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing first and PROTAC degraders second, treating both as new chemical modalities that changed what biologists and drug developers can do, and notes that the field leans toward Medicine for sequencing.
responses.response: I agree that induced-proximity degraders and base editors are important, and that their mechanisms are chemically well defined. My difficulty is the fragmented credit, for PROTACs between Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli and the cereblon and glue strand, and for base editing between Liu, his trainees and Nishida and Kondo. A prize on C-N coupling has no comparable ambiguity. If the committee prefers a two-part prize, I could support pairing a method from this group with C-N coupling, but only if the laureate list stays at three.

uncertainties: Whether the 2010 Pd cross-coupling prize makes C-N coupling look redundant to a majority of the committee.
Exact precedence of Kosugi's tin-amide aminations relative to the Buchwald and Hartwig reports, which I have not verified.
Whether PROTAC or base-editing credit can be partitioned fairly within three names, which determines how seriously I should weigh them as alternatives.
Whether a two-person synthetic methodology prize can gather enough support, since only two members ranked it in the openings.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known institutional or personal tie to Buchwald, Hartwig or Kosugi, and I am not a close collaborator of the other credited names. My lineage from Masamune's group at MIT is a general stereocontrolled synthesis tradition and not a connection to any shortlisted candidate.
